about: The model

Pay per lead is a simple idea. You pay for each enquiry that is delivered to your firm and matches the criteria you agreed. You do not pay for clicks on adverts, for impressions, for a share of a media budget or for someone's time managing campaigns. If no matching enquiry comes in, there is nothing to pay for.

The model suits law firms well because legal work is high value and enquiries are relatively rare. A firm might need only a handful of new instructions a month in a practice area to make a real difference to its income. Paying for those enquiries directly, rather than for the thousands of clicks and impressions it can take to produce them, puts the focus on the thing that actually matters to the firm.

With Leaflegal, the price of each lead is agreed with your firm before you start. It depends on the practice areas, matter types and locations you choose and the volume you want. Once it is agreed, you know exactly what each lead costs, which makes it straightforward to plan a budget and to measure what you get back.

In most forms of legal marketing, the firm carries the risk that the money spent will not produce enquiries. A month of paid search can bring in a stream of people looking for free advice. A directory listing can produce nothing at all. With pay per lead, Leaflegal carries the cost and risk of running the campaigns. You pay only for enquiries that reach you and fit what you asked for.

A lead is an enquiry from a named person or business, in a practice area, matter type and location you have chosen, with a verified UK mobile number and email address, confirmation they want paid help and a record of their consent to be contacted by a firm. It is sent to your firm only and never resold.

about.h3: What you are not paying for

about: You are not paying for an instruction. Some clients will compare firms, some will decide not to proceed and some will not accept your fees. A lead remains valid if the client chooses another firm or does not go ahead. What you are paying for is a fair chance to win the work, delivered quickly and exclusively.

There is no software to subscribe to and no login. Leads arrive by email or in your CRM. Any costs beyond the price per lead are explained in your proposal before you commit, so nothing comes as a surprise.
Other models
Law firms can pay for marketing in several ways. Each spreads cost and risk differently. It helps to understand them side by side.

With paid search and many social campaigns, you pay each time someone clicks on an advert. Legal keywords are among the most expensive to bid on, and many clicks never become enquiries. Someone has to choose keywords, write adverts, build landing pages, filter out unsuitable searches and watch spend closely. The firm carries all the risk that clicks do not turn into enquiries.

Many marketing agencies charge a monthly fee for managing campaigns, on top of the advertising spend itself. A good agency can be worth it, but the firm pays whether or not the campaigns work in a given month, and it can take time to see whether they do.
Directories usually charge a fixed fee for a listing or a premium position. Enquiries may come, or they may not, and they are often shared between several firms on the same page.
Some lead services charge per lead but send each enquiry to several firms. The price looks lower, but each firm is buying a share of a chance rather than the whole of one.

With Leaflegal, you pay a known price for each exclusive enquiry that matches your criteria. You do not manage campaigns or pay for clicks. The trade off is that the price per lead is higher than the cost of a single click, because a lead is a finished enquiry rather than a visit to a web page.

There is also a hidden cost in every model that needs managing. Someone at the firm has to brief an agency, check reports, approve adverts or chase directory listings. With pay per lead, that time is mostly replaced by a short conversation about your criteria and the occasional update when your needs change.
Many firms use pay per lead alongside their own website, referrals and sometimes their own paid search. The value of pay per lead is that it adds volume you can predict and control.
Price factors
We agree a price with each firm rather than publishing a list, because the value of a legal lead varies a great deal. Three things matter most.

Some matters are worth more to a firm than others. A contested family finances enquiry usually leads to more work, over a longer period, than a simple remortgage. A licence review hearing for a busy venue is a different proposition from a personal licence application. Matters that are harder to generate, or that tend to bring in higher fees, are priced accordingly.

A firm that covers the whole of England and Wales will match more enquiries than a firm that covers one town. Narrow coverage around a single office can be very valuable to the firm, but it produces fewer matches and can take more campaign work to fill. Coverage is reflected in the price.
The number of leads you want each month affects how we plan campaigns for your criteria. Volume is part of the conversation we have when putting your proposal together.

about.h3: What does not affect the price

about: Your price does not change from day to day because another firm is willing to pay more. There is no auction and no bidding. Once your price is agreed, it applies to every lead that matches your criteria until you and we agree something different.
If you take leads in more than one practice area, each area has its own price. A firm taking conveyancing and family leads will have a price for each, reflecting the difference in the work involved.

On your call we will ask about the work you want, where you want it and how many enquiries your team can handle. We will explain how those choices affect the price and the likely volume, and suggest where small changes might make a big difference. For example, adding a neighbouring county or a related matter type can sometimes make a narrow set of criteria far more workable. Your proposal sets out the result in writing.
Volume and control

Pay per lead only works well if you can control how many leads you receive. Too few and you cannot judge the results. Too many and your team cannot call them back quickly, which wastes both the leads and the money spent on them.

The minimum is 10 leads a month. That is enough for a firm to see the quality of the enquiries and how they fit with its intake process. Below that, results can swing a great deal from month to month for reasons that have nothing to do with lead quality.

Above the minimum, you set a cap. Once you reach it, we stop matching to your firm until the next month. The cap is also your maximum spend for the month, because you only pay for leads delivered within it.
You can raise or lower your cap whenever you need to. Firms often lower it when a fee earner is on leave and raise it when a new member of the team joins.
If your team is at capacity, you can pause altogether. While you are paused, you receive no leads and pay nothing. When you are ready, tell us and we will start matching to you again.

We cannot guarantee exact volumes, because they depend on how many people enquire and how closely they match your criteria. When we agree your criteria, we will give you an honest view of likely volumes. If your criteria are narrow, we will tell you.

The right cap is the number your team can call back within minutes, on a normal working day, without other work suffering. A useful way to set it is to count the fee earners or intake staff who will handle leads, think about how many new matters each can realistically open in a month and work back from there. It is better to start a little low and raise your cap than to start high and leave leads waiting.
Invalid leads
Paying per lead raises a fair question. What happens when a lead is not what it should be? Your partner agreement answers that before your first lead is delivered.

Your agreement defines an invalid lead. Typical examples are a lead with wrong contact details, so that the client cannot be reached on the number or email given, or a lead that falls outside the practice areas, matter types or locations agreed with you.

about.h3: What does not count as invalid

about: A lead is still valid if the client chooses another firm, decides not to proceed, cannot afford your fees or does not answer your first call. These are normal parts of working with private client enquiries. Pay per lead means paying for a fair chance to win the work, not for a guaranteed instruction.

Your agreement sets a review period for raising an invalid lead. Tell us within that time, with a short note of what was wrong. Where a lead is genuinely invalid, we deal with it as your agreement sets out.

about.h3: Why the rules are written down

about: Having the rules in writing from the start avoids disagreement later. Your team knows what to report, and we know what we have agreed to. It also helps us spot patterns. If a particular campaign or matter type keeps producing invalid leads, we want to know so we can fix it.

Most firms find that invalid leads are a small part of the picture, but it still pays to have a routine. Ask whoever handles new leads to flag anything that looks wrong on the first call, such as a number that does not connect or a matter clearly outside your criteria. Collect those flags in one place and send them to us within the review period. A short, regular note is easier for everyone than a long list at the end of the month.
Measuring return

One of the strengths of pay per lead is that the cost side of the calculation is simple. Each lead has an agreed price. What you need to add is a clear record of what happens to each lead after it arrives.

Keep a simple log with the date each lead arrived, when it was first called, whether you spoke to the client, whether they instructed and the fee the matter brought in. A spreadsheet or a field in your CRM is enough.

about.h3: Look at it by practice area

about: Compare results by practice area and matter type rather than as one figure. A family team and a conveyancing team will see different patterns, and the useful decisions usually sit at that level.

about.h3: Think about the cost per instruction

about: Divide what you spent on leads in a period by the number of instructions they produced. Compare that with the fees those instructions brought in and with what an instruction costs you through other channels. This gives a much clearer picture than the price per lead alone.
Some matters instruct on the first call. Others take weeks while clients gather documents, talk to family or save for fees. Give each month's leads time to mature before judging them.
Tell us which leads converted and which did not. We use that feedback to adjust your criteria so that more of your spend goes on the enquiries that work best for you.
Leaflegal does not charge clients anything. They are told we are paid by the firms we introduce them to. To see what pay per lead would cost for your criteria, apply to become a partner firm.
faqs: How it works
What is pay per lead for law firms?

It is a way of paying for marketing where the firm pays for each enquiry delivered to it, rather than for clicks, impressions or campaign management. With Leaflegal, each lead is an exclusive enquiry that matches your agreed practice areas, matter types and locations, at a price agreed before you start.
When do I pay for a lead?

You pay for leads delivered to your firm that match your agreed criteria. How and when you are billed is set out in your partner agreement, which you see and agree before your first lead. There is no charge for enquiries that do not reach you. Keep your own record of leads received so you can check bills easily.
Do I pay for leads that do not convert?

Yes, as long as they are valid. A lead stays valid if the client chooses another firm, decides not to proceed or does not accept your fees. Pay per lead covers the cost of producing a qualified, exclusive enquiry. It is not a guarantee of instructions, and no honest lead provider can offer one.
Is pay per lead the same as pay per instruction?

No. Pay per lead means paying for each qualified enquiry, whether or not it becomes an instruction. Leaflegal charges per lead. Firms should take their own view on how any payment arrangement with an introducer sits with their regulator's rules. Your price per lead is agreed in advance and does not depend on whether the client instructs you or on the fees you earn from the matter.
Do I need to manage any campaigns?

No. Leaflegal runs the campaigns, the enquiry forms and the checks. You agree your criteria and price, then receive leads as they come in. You do not need to choose keywords, write adverts or watch advertising budgets. Your part is calling leads quickly and telling us which ones turn into instructions, so we can refine your criteria over time.
Is there a login or dashboard?

No. There is no online platform. Leads arrive by email or in your CRM, and changes to your criteria, cap or pause status are made by contacting our team. Many firms prefer it, because there is nothing new for their team to learn. Our team handles changes for you, usually by email or phone.
Can I use pay per lead alongside my own marketing?

Yes, and most firms do. Your website, reputation and referrers usually bring in some work on their own. Pay per lead adds a source of enquiries you can turn up or down as your capacity changes. Because each lead has a known cost, it is easy to compare with what your other channels cost you.
Price
How much does each lead cost?

The price is agreed with your firm before you start. It depends on the practice areas, matter types and locations you choose and the volume you want. We do not publish prices because they vary widely. After a 30-minute call we put a proposal together for you. There is no obligation.
Why do prices vary between practice areas?

Because the value of an enquiry varies. A contested family finances matter usually brings more work than a simple remortgage, and some matter types are harder to generate than others. Pricing each area separately means you are not paying the same for very different kinds of work. We explain how on your call.
Does my location affect the price?

Yes. Narrow coverage around one office produces fewer matches than regional or national coverage and can take more campaign work to fill. Your locations are part of the conversation when we agree your price. Wider coverage tends to produce more matches and more predictable volumes. We will explain how your chosen locations affect both price and volume before you commit.
Can the price go up without warning?

No. There is no auction or bidding. Your price is agreed in advance and applies to every lead that matches your criteria until you and we agree a change. Pricing is set out in your partner agreement. If your criteria change a great deal, for example because you add a new practice area, we will agree any change in price with you in writing first.
Is there a setup fee?

Any costs beyond the price per lead are explained in your proposal before you commit. You will know exactly what you are agreeing to before your first lead is delivered. If there is nothing beyond the price per lead, the proposal will say so. Either way, it is all written into your partner agreement before you start.
Do you charge clients as well?

No. Leaflegal does not charge clients anything. The firm pays for the introduction and the client agrees fees directly with the firm. Clients are told that Leaflegal is paid by the firms it introduces. The client is free to decide whether to instruct you, and our arrangement with your firm does not change what they pay you.
Will my price be different for each practice area?

Yes, if you take leads in more than one area. Each area has its own price, reflecting the difference in the work and the cost of producing the enquiries. Your proposal sets out the price for each area you choose, and your partner agreement records it. You can add an area later.
Volume and spend
Is there a minimum number of leads?

Yes, the minimum is 10 leads a month. That gives you enough enquiries to judge quality and see how they fit with your intake. Above that, you set your own monthly cap. Below that, results can swing a lot from month to month for reasons that have nothing to do with lead quality. Many firms start near the minimum and raise their cap later.
Can I set a maximum spend?

Yes, through your monthly cap. Once you reach it, we stop matching to your firm until the next month. Because you only pay for leads delivered, your cap also sets your maximum spend on leads for the month. You can change your cap at any time, so your maximum spend can follow your team's capacity through the year.
Can I change my volume?

Yes, at any time. Many firms adjust their cap through the year, lowering it during holidays or busy periods and raising it when a new fee earner joins or a team has capacity. Just tell our team. There is no charge for changing your cap, and changes apply to the leads that follow.
Can I pause?

Yes. While you are paused you receive no leads and pay nothing for leads. Pausing does not affect your criteria or agreed price. When you are ready, tell us and we will start matching to your firm again. Pausing is a normal part of how firms use the service, particularly around holidays and busy periods.
Do you guarantee a number of leads?

We cannot guarantee exact volumes, because they depend on how many people enquire and how closely they match your criteria. We will give you an honest view of likely volumes when we agree your criteria, and tell you if your criteria are likely to limit them. Wider criteria usually mean more predictable volumes.
What happens if I receive fewer leads than my cap?

You only pay for the leads you receive. If volumes are lower than expected, talk to us. We can look at whether widening your locations or matter types would help, or whether demand in your area is simply lower at that time. Your cap is a ceiling, not a target, and there is no charge for leads you did not receive.
Invalid leads
What counts as an invalid lead?

Your partner agreement defines it. Typical examples are a lead with wrong contact details or one that falls outside the practice areas, matter types or locations agreed with you. A lead is not invalid just because the client chose another firm or did not proceed. Having the test in writing avoids disagreement later.
How do I report an invalid lead?

Tell us within the review period set out in your partner agreement, with a short note explaining the problem. Where a lead is genuinely invalid, we deal with it as your agreement sets out. A short note is enough, such as the number not connecting or the matter being outside your criteria. Reporting promptly also helps us find and fix any cause.
What if a client does not answer?

An unanswered call does not make a lead invalid. Many clients are at work, driving or cautious about unknown numbers. Leave a voicemail, send an email and a text, and try again later the same day and the next morning. If the number turns out to be wrong, that is a different matter and can be raised as invalid.
What if the client says they did not enquire?

Each lead comes with the consent wording the client agreed to and the time they agreed. People sometimes forget, especially if they enquired late at night. If a lead appears not to be genuine, raise it within the review period and we will look into it. A polite reminder of when they enquired usually helps.
Can I raise an invalid lead after the review period?

The review period is set out in your partner agreement so that problems are raised while the details are fresh. It is worth checking new leads promptly and reporting anything wrong straight away. If something unusual happens, talk to us, but the agreement is what governs how invalid leads are handled.
Return on spend
How do I work out whether pay per lead is worth it?

Track each lead from arrival to outcome. Over a period, divide what you spent on leads by the instructions they produced, then compare that with the fees those instructions brought in and with your costs through other channels. Look at it by practice area, and give leads time to mature.
How long before I can judge results?

It depends on the practice area. Deadline driven matters such as licence reviews or immigration refusals often instruct quickly. Conveyancing and family matters can take longer. Most firms want at least a couple of months of leads, with time for later instructions, before drawing firm conclusions. Look at results by practice area.
What makes the biggest difference to return?

What happens after the lead arrives. Firms that call within minutes, use what the client has told us, explain the introduction, are clear about fees and follow up properly tend to win more of their leads. Your intake process matters as much as the leads themselves. Feedback helps us too.
Will you help me improve my results?

Yes. Tell us which leads converted and which did not. We use that feedback to refine your matter types and locations, and we are happy to share what we see working for firms in general, without sharing any other firm's details. Improving your results is in our interest as well as yours, because firms that win work from their leads tend to stay and grow their volume.
Should I count leads that instruct months later?

Yes. Some clients come back weeks or months after the first call, once they have sold a house, gathered documents or reached a decision. Keep those leads in your records and link them to the original enquiry. Leaving them out would make your return look worse than it really is.
